About: Free-Body Diagram Builder

Source

Lecture
L4 — Forces & Newton's Laws (companion to the Forces on Objects Explorer)
Simulation
Free-Body Diagram Builder — reusable tool, embeddable inside other sims
Concept
Every real force on a body is attributed to an agent; F_net = Σ F_i = m a decides the motion.
Serves
Identifying particles and the real forces on each; predicting motion from a self-built FBD before net-force reveal.
Inquiry
Orient → Build (agent-labelled arrows) → Predict acceleration → Check against known-good solution.
Misconception target
Inventing agent-less forces (e.g. "force of motion"); confusing centripetal (real, inward, inertial frame) with centrifugal (fictitious, outward, rotating frame); confusing third-law pairs (they act on different bodies); omitting fictitious forces in a rotating frame.
Notation
Fg = mg for gravitational weight; N = normal; T = tension; f = friction; Fapp = applied contact push/pull; Fcf = centrifugal (rotating frame only); Fcor = Coriolis (rotating frame only). Canvas angle convention: 0° = right, 90° = up.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Orient to the scenario

Read the scene at the top of the canvas. A block sitting on a table, at rest. The body — the thing whose FBD you'll build — carries a dashed outline.

Before you draw any arrows: is this scenario in an inertial or rotating frame?

2 · Predict — how many forces?

The block rests on the table. Count the real forces acting on it — every real force needs an agent, an object that exerts it.

3 · Predict the motion

From your FBD (net force is still hidden), which way — if at all — does the block accelerate?

4 · Check & reveal

Committing here checks your FBD against the physics solution and reveals the net force. What will the reveal show for this block?

5 · Free build

The stepper is done. Pick any scenario and keep building. Untick Grade my diagram (Check & result panel) to explore freely without grading.

Just-in-time reminders will appear in the grading banner when relevant — every arrow needs an agent, and third-law pairs act on two different bodies.

01

At a glance

A block sits on a table. You draw the force arrows on it, name the body that exerts each one, and ask the sim to check the diagram. The sim then shows the net force and the motion that follows.

What you'll learn

  • How to pick one body and a frame before you draw.
  • How to tell a real force from an invented one.
  • How the forces on a body fix its acceleration.
The starting scene: one block, the dashed outline around it, and the angle convention for arrows.

What's on screen

  • Dashed outline: the one body the diagram is about.
  • Arrow colours: gravity, normal, tension, friction, applied, fictitious.
See itOpen the sim on the block, with no arrows yet. Watch for: the dashed outline around the block, labelled body, with m = 2.0 kg inside it.

Fixed: g = 9.8 m/s², static friction μs = 0.6, orbit radius 2.0 m. Angles are measured from the right, counter-clockwise: 0° is right, 90° is up.

03

Choose the frame first, and draw only the forces in it

A free-body diagram is about one body, and it holds only the forces that other bodies exert on it. The vector sum of those forces gives the acceleration:

F⃗net = ΣF⃗i = m a⃗
This holds in an inertial frame, where a body with no net force keeps its velocity.

A table that is not turning gives an inertial frame, so the block, stack, incline, two-body and pendulum scenes are all drawn in the inertial frame. The sim greys out the Rotating button in those scenes. Only the Orbit scene lets you choose a rotating frame, and section 08 shows what changes there.

See itSwitch the scenario to Orbit and read the Reference frame panel. Watch for: the Rotating button is now live, with a note that the body is at rest in that frame.
04

Every real force has an agent, and the block has two

A real force always has an agent: a body that touches the object, or pulls on it from a distance. "Motion", "momentum" and "inertia" are not agents, so they never get an arrow.

Our block rests on the table, and only two bodies act on it:

  • Gravity: the Earth pulls it down, with weight mg = 2.0 × 9.8 = 19.6 N (angle 270°).
  • Normal: the table pushes it up, perpendicular to the surface, here 19.6 N (angle 90°).

There is no third arrow for "the force that keeps it in place": no body is exerting one. Each arrow needs its agent typed in the editor.

See itBuild the block's diagram with two arrows and read the list. Watch for: gravity 19.6 N, agent Earth, and normal 19.6 N, agent table, drawn from the body.
05

The net force sets the acceleration

Add the arrows as vectors. For the block, 19.6 N up and 19.6 N down give Fnet = 0. Then a = Fnet/m = 0, and the block stays at rest.

The two forces cancel because the block is not accelerating, not because of the third law. Weight and normal act on the same body, so they cannot be a third-law pair. The partner of the weight is the block's own pull on the Earth.

After a correct check the readouts show three values: |Fnet|, its direction, and the acceleration a = |Fnet|/m. A balanced diagram reads (balanced) for the direction.

See itCheck the two-arrow diagram of the block. Watch for: ✓ Correct FBD, then |Fnet| = 0.00 N, direction (balanced) and a = 0.00 m/s².
06

On a slope the weight splits along and across the surface

On the incline the normal force is perpendicular to the slope, so it no longer opposes gravity directly. Gravity splits into two parts:

  • Across the slope, N = mg cos θ = 2 × 9.8 × cos 25° = 17.76 N. This sets the normal force.
  • Along the slope, mg sin θ = 2 × 9.8 × sin 25° = 8.28 N, pointing down the slope.

With only gravity and the normal, the net force is 8.28 N down the slope, so a = g sin θ = 4.14 m/s². Static friction up the slope is optional in the sim. To hold the block it must supply 8.28 N, and it can supply at most μsN = 0.6 × 17.76 = 10.66 N, so the check accepts a diagram with friction too.

m θ

These sliders move the sim too.

See itOn the incline at 25°, check a diagram with gravity and normal only. Watch for: |Fnet| = 8.28 N at −25°, down the slope, and a = 4.14 m/s².
See itAdd a friction arrow of 8.28 N up the slope, at 155°. Watch for: the net force falls to 0.00 N, so the block is held.
07

A third-law pair acts on two different bodies

In the two-body scene, box A pushes box B along a smooth floor. Draw the diagram for B. It feels three forces:

  • Gravity, 19.6 N down, agent Earth.
  • Normal, 19.6 N up, agent floor.
  • The push from A, Fapp = 5.0 N to the right (angle 0°), agent box A.

The vertical forces cancel, so Fnet = 5.0 N and a = 5.0/2 = 2.5 m/s². The push that B exerts back on A has the same size and the opposite direction. It acts on A, so it is not on B's diagram. The sim treats the floor as frictionless.

See itIn the Two-body scene, check B's three-arrow diagram. Watch for: |Fnet| = 5.00 N at 0° and a = 2.50 m/s², with no arrow for the push on A.
08

In a rotating frame a fictitious force appears

In the Orbit scene a body circles a central body at radius R = 2.0 m with turning rate ω. The inward force needed is mω²R, which is 2 × 1² × 2.0 = 4.0 N at the defaults.

  • Inertial frame. Gravity from the central body is the only force, 4.0 N toward the centre. The inward acceleration, a = ω²R = 2 m/s², is a result of that force and not a second arrow.
  • Rotating frame. The body is at rest, so gravity 4.0 N inward is balanced by a fictitious centrifugal force of 4.0 N outward. The Coriolis force −2mω × v′ is zero because v′ = 0.

Fictitious forces have no agent, since no body exerts them. They are the price of using an accelerating frame.

See itIn the Orbit scene choose the Rotating frame and check gravity plus centrifugal. Watch for: two equal and opposite red and blue arrows of 4.0 N, and |Fnet| = 0.00 N.
09

Summary

In one line. A free-body diagram shows every real force on one body, each with the body that exerts it.

Key points

  • Pick one body and a frame. Each real force has an agent.
  • The vector sum gives a = Fnet/m. On a slope, resolve the weight along and across it.
  • A third-law pair acts on two bodies, so only one of the two is on your diagram.
  • In a rotating frame add fictitious forces. In an inertial frame never do.

Common mix-ups

  • "The normal force is the reaction to gravity." Both act on the same body, so they are not a third-law pair.
  • "Circular motion needs a centripetal arrow." In an inertial frame the real forces already give the inward acceleration.
  • "The block on a slope needs friction to feel a normal force." The normal exists with no friction at all.

Things to try on your own

  • Raise θ to 40° and find where the friction needed exceeds μsN.
  • Change ω to 2 rad/s in Orbit and predict the new inward force.
  • Add a centrifugal arrow in the inertial frame and read the explanation.
